Chapter Two: The Power and Pressure of Creating Propaganda.
You know, in a world where words can cut as deep as any weapon, the people who shape those words hold a truly unusual power. Imagine being one of those writers or artists—you're not just creating stories or poems. No, you're actually guarding the official truth, weaving this endless tapestry of loyalty that touches every corner of daily life.
Picture this: there’s a young poet, someone whose talent stands out so much, he's handpicked from the crowd. Suddenly, he’s invited into an elite circle—a group whose words are read not just by ordinary people, but by the most powerful leaders in the country. It sounds like a dream, right? The honor is huge. But so is the responsibility.
Every poem and every short story must serve a clear purpose. Glorify the leader. Inspire devotion. Erase any shadow of doubt. It’s not just about beautiful language; it’s about shaping hearts and minds.
The work itself is demanding—there’s no getting around that. But there are privileges, too. Better meals, warmer clothes, a sense that what you do actually matters. But here’s the catch: these rewards are never guaranteed. The pressure to deliver is constant. And if you slip up? If you write a phrase that could be read the wrong way, or use a metaphor that sounds off? Suddenly, you’re facing suspicion, maybe even an investigation. Sometimes, it can ruin you.
Inside the writers’ offices, there’s this odd mix of camaraderie and tension. Sure, people share jokes and stories. But underneath, everyone’s careful. It’s hard to trust anyone, because today’s friend could become tomorrow’s informant. The walls are thin, and rumors seem to fly faster than you can blink.
Creating propaganda—it’s part art, part science. Writers pore over the leader’s speeches, analyzing every word for clues about what’s “in line” right now. Then they build stories that blend history with myth, turning everyday events into grand tales of heroism and sacrifice. The goal? Not just to inform, but to shape how people think. To make any other reality feel impossible.
For our poet, this work is a mix of pride and exhaustion. There’s a thrill in knowing millions will read your words. But there’s also this creeping unease. The more he learns about how the system really works, the bigger the gap he sees between the stories he tells and the life he actually lives. Those contradictions start to pile up, and suddenly, keeping quiet feels like its own kind of burden.
Most folks outside this circle will never see the hidden side of propaganda. They read the poems, watch the plays, and believe in the world those stories paint. But for the creators, it’s not so simple. They know that every word is a choice, and every choice carries risk.
Over time, the poet starts to wonder about his own place in all this. Is it really possible to serve the truth, while you’re serving the state? Can art survive when it’s used to control rather than to inspire? These questions stick with him, growing louder every single day.
